headings.title: Definition and Overview of Gishiri Cut
headings.content: Gishiri cut is a traditional surgical practice found mostly in northern Nigeria and some neighboring West African countries. The term **'gishiri'** is the Hausa word for salt. Practitioners perform this procedure using a sharp instrument like a razor blade or knife to make incisions inside the vagina. This act stems from the mistaken belief that vaginal or lower abdominal symptoms stem from a hardened or blocked salt deposit. Victims are often young girls or women experiencing obstructed labor, infertility, dysmenorrhea, or general pelvic discomfort. The practice causes severe physical trauma without any physiological benefit. Nurses working in affected communities must understand this harmful traditional practice to identify patients who have undergone the procedure.

headings.title: Cultural Drivers and Societal Context
headings.content: Harmful traditional practices like the gishiri cut persist due to deep-seated cultural beliefs, lack of formal education, and poor access to orthodox healthcare services. Rural communities often rely heavily on traditional birth attendants and local healers who command high social respect. Women may lack autonomy over their bodies and health choices, leaving them vulnerable to decisions made by family elders or husbands. When orthodox medical services are expensive or physically distant, traditional remedies become the default option. Addressing this practice requires culturally sensitive community engagement rather than outright condemnation, which often drives the practice underground.

headings.title: Anatomical Structures Affected
headings.content:
The incisions made during a gishiri cut target the vaginal walls, often extending deeply into surrounding tissues depending on the condition being treated. 

- **Anterior vaginal wall**: Commonly cut when practitioners attempt to relieve obstructed labor or urinary retention, frequently resulting in vesicovaginal fistula.
- **Posterior vaginal wall**: Incised for lower back pain or bowel issues, risking rectovaginal fistula.
- **Vaginal fornices and cervix**: Damaged during deep cuts intended to treat infertility or lower abdominal swelling.

These delicate structures contain rich vascular and neural networks, making them highly vulnerable to profuse bleeding and permanent scarring.

headings.title: Immediate and Long-Term Complications
headings.content:
| Timeline | Primary Complications |
| :--- | :--- |
| Immediate | Severe hemorrhage, excruciating pain, profound shock, local sepsis |
| Long-Term | Vesicovaginal fistula (VVF), rectovaginal fistula, severe vaginal scarring, dyspareunia, secondary infertility |

The physical damage extends beyond physical scars, leaving patients with devastating social consequences. Women suffering from continuous urinary or fecal incontinence due to fistulas often face stigmatization, divorce, and social isolation from their communities.

headings.title: Clinical Assessment and Diagnosis in Nursing
headings.content: Nurses must maintain a high index of suspicion when evaluating women from endemic regions who present with unexplained pelvic pain, bleeding, or incontinence. Assessment begins with a thorough history focusing on obstetric events, traditional treatments, and the onset of symptoms. A gentle physical examination is necessary, though patients may experience severe anxiety or pain due to past trauma. Inspect the perineum and vaginal vault using appropriate lighting and privacy. Look out for scar tissue, structural distortion, or abnormal openings between the vagina and the bladder or rectum. Document all findings objectively and build a trusting nurse-patient relationship to encourage open communication.

headings.title: Medical, Surgical, and Nursing Management
headings.content: Management of complications arising from gishiri cuts requires a multidisciplinary approach involving nurses, general practitioners, and reconstructive surgeons. Acute bleeding requires immediate resuscitation with intravenous fluids, blood transfusion, and local hemostasis. Infection control relies on prescribed broad-spectrum antibiotics and proper wound care. Patients with fistulas require specialized surgical repair, often deferred until local inflammation subsides. Nursing care includes managing catheters, monitoring intake and output, providing nutritional support, and offering empathetic psychological counseling to help patients cope with trauma and stigma.

headings.title: Prevention, Advocacy, and Community Health Nursing
headings.content: Eradicating harmful practices like the gishiri cut requires community-level health education and grassroots advocacy. Community health nurses play a pivotal role by conducting awareness campaigns that explain the real anatomical and physiological causes of diseases. Engaging community leaders, religious figures, and reformed traditional birth attendants helps spread accurate health information. Nurses must also advocate for girl-child education and improved maternal health services in rural areas. Empowering women economically and socially reduces their reliance on unsafe traditional practices and promotes better healthcare-seeking behaviors.
